Issued at 253 AM CDT Tue Oct 13 2026

Current H5 analysis shows a deep mid/upper level low centered
over Nevada with attendant troughing into the Desert Southwest.
At the surface, a cold front has mostly stalled across northern
Missouri into NE Kansas. South of the front, temperatures this
early morning range in the upper 60s to lower 70s, which is 20
to 25 degrees above normal for October 13th. The aforementioned
mid/upper low will move slowly east southeast across the Great
Basin and Desert Southwest through the day today, with a lee
surface cyclone moving into the south central High Plains this
afternoon and evening downstream of the upper trough. Meanwhile,
the pseudo stationary cold front should remain in place across
northern MO into eastern Kansas. A southwesterly oriented belt
of 35 to 55 knot H5 winds is progged to overspread the CWA by 
this afternoon and evening, and with afternoon temperatures
soaring into the upper 80s to lower 90s for locations south of
the cold front (decent chance of breaking the record high in
Kansas City today) and rich low level moisture, moderate 
instability should be in place to the tune of 1500 to 2500 J/kg 
of ML CAPE. Initially discrete convection is projected to 
develop by mid to late afternoon across east- central Kansas, 
likely growing upscale into clusters as storms move eastward 
toward our CWA by early evening. Given the pairing of sufficient
deep layer shear and moderate buoyancy, updrafts should be 
relatively well organized as they moving into our CWA this 
evening, with large hail and damaging wind gusts being the 
primary hazards. However, there will likely be a modest uptick 
in low level shear/SRH by this evening near the surface front, 
which has prompted SPC to upgrade portions of our CWA to a 2% 
tornado risk. Another round of convection is likely to develop 
across south central KS by this evening behind the first round, 
with this likely growing upscale into an MCS as it moves into 
southern portions of the CWA late tonight into early Wednesday 
morning. With PWATs on the order of 1.8" to 2" this evening and 
increasing further to 2" to 2.2" (per the SPC HREF) across 
southern portions of the CWA late tonight into early Wednesday, 
locally moderate to heavy rainfall will be possible, with HREF 
probability matched means on the order of 2" to 3" across 
portions of the region, especially for areas south of the KC 
metro, with locally higher amounts certainly possible. Thus, in 
collaboration with neighboring offices, have went ahead and 
hoisted a flood watch from 7 pm this evening through 10 AM 
Wednesday for areas south and southeast of the KC metro. 
Depending on how guidance trends this morning and afternoon, it 
is possible that the watch could be expanded northward 
(including for the KC metro). 

The cold front should finally push south through most (if not
all) of the CWA by Wednesday afternoon. While the forecast still
shows chance PoPs (around 50 percent or so) throughout the
daytime hours of Wednesday, quite a bit of high res guidance
suggests we may be by and large dry other than some drizzle or
light stratiform rain, with the best chances for any 
appreciable rainfall (0.25" or more) across our far southern 
areas closer to the surface cold front. By Wednesday night into
early Thursday morning, the western trough is projected to eject
across the south central Plains, which should help generate
widespread showers (with some embedded thunderstorms) across the
CWA late Wednesday night into Thursday morning (PoPs are 90 to
100% across much of the CWA from 1 AM to 1 PM Thursday). This
should bring another inch or so of rainfall across much of the 
region. Rain should exit from west to east by Thursday evening
as the mid/upper trough scoots off into the Great Lakes region
and the cold front races well to the east southeast, with skies
mostly clearing from west to east by Friday morning. Colder and
much drier air will infiltrate the CWA on Friday, with highs
only in the upper 50s to lower 60s and dew points in the upper
30s to lower 40s. Meanwhile, a 1040 mb high centered over the
central High Plains and a 1004 mb low centered over the eastern
Great Lakes will yield a strong pressure gradient across the
area, with northerly winds on the order of 20 mph with gusts up
to 30 mph Friday morning into early Friday afternoon. The
pressure gradient should begin to subside by later Friday
afternoon as the surface high slides eastward closer to our CWA.
By Friday night, the surface high should be centered directly
overhead, yielding calm winds, clear skies, and low dew points.
This will make for excellent radiational cooling conditions, and
temperatures early Saturday morning should fall into the mid to
upper 30s across the region (warmer of course across the KC
urban head island). This should yield some patchy frost across
the area, especially northern Missouri where temperatures should
be the coldest. 

Saturday should be a beautiful mid October
